images.alt: A Dragon 32 home computer in its cream case, photographed from the front with its full-travel keyboard visible
images.caption: The Dragon 32, built in Port Talbot to Motorola's own reference design around the MC6809E processor.
images.author: Liftarn, Editing by: Bill Bertram (Pixel8)

images.alt: A Dragon 32 computer on display at a vintage computing exhibition, shown from the front with its keyboard and cartridge slot
images.caption: Full-travel keys were one of the Dragon's genuine strengths, at a time when rival machines were selling rubber membranes.
images.author: AUIC Oficial

images.alt: Close view of a Dragon 32 computer casing showing its keyboard and Dragon Data branding
images.caption: Dragon Data set up in South Wales in 1982 to build a home computer for Britain's boom, priced just under £200.
images.author: Wolfgang Stief from Tittmoning, Germany

images.alt: A Dragon 32 computer displayed at a retro computing expo, shown at an angle with its case and keyboard visible
images.caption: Underneath the case sat an MC6809E, an 8-bit processor with two accumulators, hardware multiply and genuinely position-independent code.
images.author: Rept0n1x

images.alt: Overhead view of a Dragon 32 computer showing the full keyboard layout and cartridge port
images.caption: The keyboard's unshifted letters are capitals — lower case comes out as inverse video, a quirk of the machine's MC6847 video chip.
images.author: Miguel Durán
